chapter_note.about: This chapter explains why averages are steadier than single values, and then uses that to build ranges for unknown quantities. The central limit theorem says sums and averages of many variables look normal, so one table covers them. Confidence intervals go z standard errors either side of an estimate, and the chi-square and t distributions take over when the spread must be estimated. DA papers average about 1.7 marks per paper from this chapter.
chapter_note.simple: A single measurement can be off by a lot, but the average of many measurements is much steadier, and the more you average the steadier it gets, though only by the square root of the count. When you add or average lots of things, the picture of the result is always the same smooth bell, whatever the things looked like. So to guess an unknown true average, you take your sample average and give a range around it, a few 'wobbles' wide. A wider range makes you more sure, and more data narrows it. When you also have to guess the spread from a small sample, the bell gets slightly fatter tails (the t curve). 95% confident describes how often the method works, not this one range. In exam words: SE = σ/√n, CLT, x-bar plus or minus z SE, chi-square and t.

cards.title: Mean and standard error of the sample mean
cards.simple: Imagine a bag of marbles with numbers on them, and you pull out a few and take their average. One marble can be anything, but an average of several marbles is steadier, because a high one and a low one cancel. The average of many averages sits at the bag's true average. How wobbly one average is, is the 'standard error', and it shrinks when you use more marbles. To make it half as wobbly you need four times as many marbles, not twice. In exam words: E[X-bar] = μ, Var(X-bar) = σ^2/n and the standard error is σ/√n.
cards.idea: Take n independent readings from a population with mean μ and spread σ, and average them. The average is **centred on μ**, and its spread is smaller than σ because highs and lows cancel. That spread, called the **standard error**, is σ divided by the square root of n.
cards.definition:
For independent $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and $\bar X=\frac1n\sum X_i$:

$$E[\bar X]=\mu,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\qquad \mathrm{SE}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$

Symbols: n is the sample size and σ is the standard deviation of one observation. The total $\sum X_i$ has mean nμ and variance nσ^2.
cards.intuition_full: The mean is a linear map: add n copies and divide by n. Expectation passes through linear maps, so E[X-bar] = (1/n)(nμ) = μ. For the variance, independent variances add, so the sum has variance nσ^2. Dividing the sum by n divides the variance by n^2, which leaves σ^2/n. That is where the square root comes from: the spread falls like 1/√n, not 1/n. Averaging helps, but with diminishing returns: going from 4 readings to 16 halves the error, and halving it again needs 64. The same formula needs independence. If readings are linked, the cross terms do not vanish and the average does not settle as quickly.

example.setup: A population takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with probabilities 0.35, 0.28, 0.18, 0.12, 0.07. Find its mean and standard deviation, then the standard error of the sample mean for n = 2, 4, 32 and 16.
steps: n = 2: the mean of the averages stays 2.28. SE = 1.25 / sqrt(2) = 0.884.
n = 32: SE = 1.25 / sqrt(32) = 0.221. The histogram of averages is now a narrow bell.
Quadruple n from 4 to 16: SE = 1.25 / 4 = 0.3125, exactly half of 0.625.

cards.title: Central limit theorem
cards.simple: Roll one die and every face 1 to 6 is equally likely, a flat picture. Add the results of two dice and the picture becomes a triangle, because 7 can happen in many more ways than 2 or 12. Add three dice and the picture is already a hump. Keep adding and the hump becomes the same smooth bell shape, no matter what shape you started with. That is why one table, the normal table, answers questions about totals and averages of many things. You only need the average and the spread of one thing. In exam words: for large n, the sum is approximately N(nμ, nσ^2) and the mean is approximately N(μ, σ^2/n).
cards.idea: Add up many independent copies of almost any random variable and the total looks like a **normal curve**. The shape of the original does not matter, only its mean and variance. So for a sum of n copies you use the normal with mean nμ and variance nσ^2, and for an average the normal with mean μ and variance σ^2/n. This is the **central limit theorem** (CLT).
cards.definition:
If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are iid with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, then for large n:

$$\sum X_i\approx N(n\mu,\,n\sigma^2),\qquad \bar X\approx N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),\qquad Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\approx N(0,1)$$

Symbols: iid means independent and identically distributed. The theorem needs a finite variance. If the population is itself normal, the result is exact for every n.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the total as many small independent nudges, some up and some down. A big total needs many nudges to line up the same way, and that is rare. Most of the time they partly cancel and you get a middling total, which is why the middle is the tallest. The mean and variance of the sum are exact for every n; the CLT adds the claim about the shape. Smoother, more symmetric starting shapes need fewer terms. Very skewed shapes need many more. A population with infinite variance, such as the Cauchy, breaks the theorem: averages of Cauchy values are as wild as one value.

example.setup: Fair dice. Look at the sum of 1, 2 and 3 dice, then use the CLT for 30 dice to find P(sum > 115). Given Φ(1.07) = 0.8577.
steps: One die: all six faces have probability 1/6, a flat shape. Mean 3.5, variance 35/12 = 2.917.
Sum of 2 dice: a triangle from 2 to 12, with 7 the most likely. Mean 7, variance 5.833.
Sum of 3 dice: already a hump from 3 to 18. Mean 10.5, variance 8.75.
Sum of 30 dice: mean 30 x 3.5 = 105, variance 30 x 35/12 = 87.5, SD = 9.354. By the CLT it is close to N(105, 87.5).
example.answer: The shape turns from flat to triangle to hump to bell. P(sum of 30 dice > 115) is about 0.1423.

cards.why: It turns questions about sums and averages of many variables of any kind into a single normal-table lookup. In GATE: approximate the probability of a binomial or Poisson sum, a sample total or a sample mean by standardising, or recognise the limit of a sum of Poisson probabilities.
how: Find the mean and variance of one term.
For a sum use nμ and nσ^2. For an average use μ and σ^2 / n.
Standardise the limit: z = (value - mean) / SD of whatever you are approximating.
Look up Φ(z), using 1 - Φ(z) for an upper tail.
For symmetric limits around the mean, use 2Φ(z) - 1.
cards.mistake: Standardising a sample mean with σ instead of σ / √n, or a sum with σ instead of σ√n. A second slip is thinking the CLT makes the data themselves normal. It only describes the sum or average.
edge_cases: Population normal: X-bar is exactly normal for any n.
Heavy skew: needs larger n before the bell appears.
Infinite variance (Cauchy): the CLT fails.
A sum of Poisson(n) probabilities up to n tends to 0.5, because the limit is Φ(0) (2026 DA Q45).
connections: Normal approximation to the binomial (next card) is the CLT for a sum of indicators.
Confidence intervals use the CLT to say X-bar is about normal.
Standardising uses the z-score from prob.continuous.

cards.title: Normal approximation to the binomial
cards.simple: Toss a coin 64 times with a one-in-four chance of heads each time and count the heads. The count is usually near 16, and the chance of exactly 20 or fewer can be found by adding up lots of terms, which is slow. Instead, draw a smooth bell curve through the bars of the histogram and measure the area under it. The bars are blocks that are each one wide, so a bar for '20' really covers 19.5 to 20.5. To include the whole 20 block, measure the bell up to 20.5, not 20. That half-step is called the continuity correction. In exam words: use N(np, np(1-p)) and move the boundary by half a unit.
cards.idea: A binomial count is a sum of n independent 0/1 results, so by the CLT it looks like a normal with mean np and variance np(1 - p). The binomial counts whole numbers, but the normal is smooth, so move each boundary half a unit to include the whole bar. This is the **continuity correction**.
cards.definition:
If $Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ with np and n(1 - p) both large (rule of thumb: at least 10):

$$Y\approx N\big(np,\;np(1-p)\big)$$

$P(Y\le k)\approx\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{k+0.5-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)$, $P(Y\ge k)\approx1-\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{k-0.5-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)$, and $P(Y=k)\approx\Phi(z_{k+0.5})-\Phi(z_{k-0.5})$.

Symbols: n trials, success probability p, k a count.
cards.intuition_full: Each binomial probability is a bar of width 1 centred on its count. The bar for 20 stretches from 19.5 to 20.5. 'At most 20' means all the bars up to and including the one at 20, so the right edge is 20.5. 'At least 36' starts from the bar at 36, whose left edge is 35.5. If you skip the correction, you cut the end bar in half and lose about half its probability. For large n each bar is tiny and the effect is small, but for tests with a given table you should include it. The approximation works best when p is near 0.5, because the binomial is then nearly symmetric. For very small p, the binomial is skewed and the normal is a poor fit (Poisson is better).

example.setup: Y ~ Binomial(64, 0.25). Use a normal approximation with continuity correction to find P(Y <= 20). Given Φ(1.30) = 0.9032.
steps: 'Y <= 20' covers the bars up to 20, whose right edge is 20.5, so use 20.5 as the boundary.
The exact binomial value is 0.9007, so the approximation is within 0.003.

how: Check np and n(1 - p) are large. Compute the mean np and SD sqrt(np(1 - p)).
Write the event in terms of whole numbers and move each boundary half a unit outward to include the full bar.
Standardise the corrected boundary: z = (boundary - np) / SD.
Use Φ for 'below', 1 - Φ for 'above', and a difference for a band.
If the question says 'use the CLT' or 'no continuity correction', skip the half-unit.
cards.mistake: Applying the correction in the wrong direction. For 'at most k' go up to k + 0.5, and for 'at least k' go down to k - 0.5. A second slip is using variance instead of SD when standardising.
edge_cases: Strict inequality: P(Y < k) = P(Y <= k - 1), so the boundary is k - 0.5.
Point probability P(Y = k): use the two edges k - 0.5 and k + 0.5.
If the question says 'use the CLT without correction', follow it, since the answer key uses that.
Small np (below about 5) or extreme p: the normal fits poorly, use the exact or Poisson value.
connections: It is the CLT for a sum of Bernoulli indicators (previous card).
The Poisson with a large mean is approximated the same way, with variance equal to the mean.
The z-test for a proportion in prob.tests uses the same normal approximation.

cards.title: z interval for a mean
cards.simple: You weigh 36 packets from a factory and find their average is 50 g. The true factory average may be a little different, since you only looked at 36. So you give a range: the average plus or minus a safety margin. The margin is a few 'wobbles' wide, where one wobble (the standard error) is the packet-to-packet spread divided by the square root of 36. If you want to be more sure, you widen the range. If you weigh more packets, you can narrow the range. In exam words: the interval is x-bar plus or minus z times σ/√n, with z = 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 for 90%, 95%, 99%.
cards.idea: A sample mean is only an estimate of μ. A **confidence interval** gives a range around it: x-bar plus and minus z standard errors. A bigger z gives more confidence but a wider range. A bigger n shrinks the standard error and so narrows the range.
cards.definition:
With σ known and X-bar approximately normal:

$$\bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$

Common values: $z=1.645$ (90%), $1.96$ (95%), $2.576$ (99%).

Symbols: x-bar is the sample mean, σ/√n is the standard error, and z is the value that leaves α/2 in each tail. The half-width $E=z\sigma/\sqrt n$ is called the margin of error.
cards.intuition_full: X-bar is approximately N(μ, σ^2/n). So with probability 95% it falls within 1.96 standard errors of μ. Turn that around: μ is within 1.96 standard errors of the observed X-bar, 95% of the time, for random samples. The number 1.96 is the z-score that leaves 2.5% in each tail. Choosing 99% instead pushes the cut to 2.576, so the interval widens. Doubling n shrinks the standard error by √2, and quadrupling it halves the interval. These three levers, confidence level, spread σ and sample size n, are the only things that change the width.

example.setup: n = 36 observations with x-bar = 50 and known σ = 12. Find the 95% interval, the 99% interval, and the 95% interval if n were 144.
steps: Standard error = σ / sqrt(n) = 12 / 6 = 2.

n = 144: SE = 12 / 12 = 1, half-width 1.96. Interval = (48.04, 51.96), half as wide as with n = 36.
Lesson: confidence costs width, and data buys narrowness. Quadrupling n halves the width.

cards.title: Interval width and sample size
cards.simple: Suppose you want to know the average weight of packets to within 2 grams, and you want to be very sure. How many packets must you weigh? The margin shrinks as you weigh more, but slowly. So rearrange the margin formula to solve for how many packets you need. Whatever the answer, if it comes out as 106.17 you cannot weigh 0.17 of a packet, and 106 would not quite be enough, so you always round up to 107. Also watch the words: 'within 2 grams' means 2 on each side, but 'width 2 grams' means only 1 on each side. In exam words: n is at least (zσ/E)^2, rounded up.
cards.idea: If you need the interval's half-width to be at most E, you can solve the interval formula for n. The required sample size grows with the **square** of z σ / E, so cutting the margin in half needs four times the data. Always **round up**.
cards.definition:
$$E=z\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\ge\left(\frac{z\,\sigma}{E}\right)^2$$

Symbols: E is the largest half-width you will accept, z the value for your confidence level and σ the population SD. Take the smallest whole number that is at least this value. If the question gives the full width W, then E = W/2.
cards.intuition_full: Start from E = z σ / √n. To make E smaller, n must grow, because n sits under a square root. Rearrange: √n = z σ / E, then square. The square explains the scaling: halve E and the right side doubles, so n quadruples. That is why very precise estimates are expensive. Rounding up matters because the formula gives the smallest real number that meets the target. Any smaller whole number would give E slightly above the target, and the next whole number is the first that works. Check the answer by substituting back.

example.setup: σ = 8. Find the smallest n so that a 99% interval (z = 2.576) has half-width at most 2.
steps: Half-width E = z σ / sqrt(n) must be at most 2.
Solve: sqrt(n) >= z σ / E, so n >= (z σ / E)^2.
Round up to the next whole number: n = 107.
Check: n = 106 gives E = 2.576 x 8 / sqrt(106) = 2.0016, just above 2. n = 107 gives E = 1.9923, which is at most 2.

cards.title: Confidence interval for a proportion
cards.simple: You ask 500 people whether they like a new phone and 140 say yes. So 28% of your sample like it. The real share in all people could be a bit different. How much? The wobble in a share depends on how close to 50-50 it is, since a split of 50-50 is the most uncertain. So the wobble is the square root of share times not-share divided by the sample size. Then add and subtract about two wobbles for a 95% range. If you do not know the share at all, assume the most uncertain case, 50%, and you will never be too small. In exam words: p-hat plus or minus z times sqrt(p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n); the worst case uses p = 0.5.
cards.idea: A proportion is an average of 0/1 answers, so the same interval idea applies. Estimate p by the sample share p-hat, estimate its standard error using p-hat, and go z standard errors each way. The standard error is largest when p is 0.5, which gives a safe worst case for planning.
cards.definition:
$$\hat p\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p\,(1-\hat p)}{n}}$$

Symbols: p-hat = x / n is the sample proportion (x successes out of n), and z is the usual 1.645, 1.96 or 2.576.

Worst case: p(1 - p) is at most 1/4, so the half-width is at most $z/(2\sqrt n)$ and the safe sample size is $n\ge\left(\dfrac{z}{2E}\right)^2$.
cards.intuition_full: A proportion is the mean of indicators with variance p(1 - p). So p-hat has variance p(1 - p) / n, and by the CLT it is approximately normal. We do not know p, so plug in p-hat in the standard error. The product p(1 - p) peaks at 0.5, where it equals 0.25, because answers are most unpredictable when the split is even. At p = 0.1 it is only 0.09. This is why a planner who knows nothing about p uses 0.25 and gets a sample size that works for every p, while someone with a rough guess can use fewer people.

Worst case for comparison: with p = 0.5 the SE would be 0.0224 and the margin 0.0438, the largest it can be for n = 500.

cards.title: Chi-square distribution
cards.simple: Take a few random numbers that are typically around 0, with a typical size of 1. Square each one so they are all positive, then add the squares. That total is a chi-square number. Adding more squares makes the total bigger on average: with 6 squares, the total averages about 6. The shape is not a mirror image: it has a long tail to the right. This turns up whenever you ask how spread out a sample is, because spread is built from squares of gaps. In exam words: chi-square with k degrees of freedom is the sum of k squared standard normals, with mean k and variance 2k.
cards.idea: Square independent standard normal numbers and add them. The total is a **chi-square** variable. The number of squares is its **degrees of freedom** k. Its mean is k and its variance is 2k, and it has a long right tail. It describes how sample variances behave.
cards.definition:
If $Z_1,\dots,Z_k$ are independent N(0, 1), then $\chi^2_k=\sum_{i=1}^kZ_i^2$, with

$$E=k,\qquad \mathrm{Var}=2k$$

For a normal sample of size n with variance σ^2: $\dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$.

Symbols: k is the degrees of freedom. S^2 is the sample variance with divisor n - 1.
cards.intuition_full: Each Z^2 has mean 1 (that is the variance of Z) and variance 2 (E[Z^4] - 1 = 3 - 1). Independent terms add, so k squares have mean k and variance 2k. The shape is skewed right because squares cannot be negative and one large Z gives a very large square. For a sample, the n deviations from the sample mean are not independent: they must add to zero. That removes one degree of freedom, so (n - 1) S^2 / σ^2 has k = n - 1. Rescaling by σ^2 turns the squared gaps into squares of standard normals.

example.setup: Z_1, ..., Z_6 are independent N(0, 1) and X = Z_1^2 + ... + Z_6^2. Then a sample of n = 9 comes from N(μ, σ^2 = 9). Find E[X], Var(X), and E[S^2] and Var(S^2).
steps: X is a sum of 6 squared standard normals, so X ~ chi-square with k = 6 degrees of freedom.
Var(X) = 2k = 12, so the SD is 3.46.
For the sample: (n - 1) S^2 / σ^2 = 8 S^2 / 9 ~ chi-square with 8 degrees of freedom. So S^2 = (9 / 8) times a chi-square(8) variable.

cards.title: t distribution
cards.simple: When you work out how far your sample average is from the true average, you need to know how spread out the population is. But often you only have your small sample to guess the spread, so your guess is itself shaky. This extra shakiness makes extreme results more likely than the plain bell curve says. The t curve is a bell curve with fatter tails to account for that. With very small samples the tails are very fat. With big samples the t curve becomes nearly the same as the bell. In exam words: T = (x-bar - μ)/(s/√n) follows t with n - 1 degrees of freedom, symmetric, heavier tails than the normal, variance k/(k - 2).
cards.idea: When σ is unknown, you replace it by the sample SD s. The statistic (X-bar - μ) / (s / √n) then follows a **t distribution** with n - 1 degrees of freedom. It looks like the standard normal but with **heavier tails**, because s adds extra uncertainty. As the degrees of freedom grow, it becomes the normal.
cards.definition:
For a normal sample of size n:

$$T=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}$$

$t_k$ is symmetric about 0, has heavier tails than N(0, 1), has variance $\dfrac{k}{k-2}$ for k > 2, and tends to N(0, 1) as k grows. It is built as $Z/\sqrt{\chi^2_k/k}$ with Z and the chi-square independent.

Symbols: k = n - 1 is the degrees of freedom.
cards.intuition_full: The ratio Z / sqrt(chi-square / k) divides a normal by a noisy estimate of its own scale. When that denominator is small by chance, the ratio blows up, and that is what creates heavy tails. With few degrees of freedom the denominator is noisy, so the tails are very heavy. As k grows, the chi-square over k concentrates near 1 and the ratio is just Z. The variance k / (k - 2) exceeds 1 and drops towards 1. It does not exist for k <= 2, and the mean does not exist for k = 1 (the Cauchy). Heavier tails also mean a lower peak, since the total area is fixed.

example.setup: Compare t with 8 degrees of freedom with the standard normal. Find the probability beyond +/-2 for each, the variance of t_8, and the variance of t_30.

Beyond +/-2: the normal has 2 x 0.0228 = 0.0455. The t_8 has 0.0805. Heavier tails mean more extreme values.
Variance of t_8 = 8 / (8 - 2) = 1.333, larger than the normal's 1.
For t_30: 30 / 28 = 1.071. With more degrees of freedom it moves close to the normal.

cards.title: Unbiased and maximum-likelihood estimators
cards.simple: Suppose you guess the spread of a population from a small sample. The spread of your sample around its own average is a bit smaller than the spread around the true average, because the sample's own average sits right inside the sample. So if you divide by the full count n, you tend to guess too low. Dividing by n - 1 instead fixes that on average. That fixed guess is called unbiased. The version that divides by n is the maximum-likelihood guess, the one that fits your sample best, and it is slightly low. Surprisingly, the square root of the unbiased variance is not unbiased for the spread. In exam words: S^2 divides by n - 1 and is unbiased, the MLE divides by n and is biased low, and S is biased.
cards.idea: An estimator is **unbiased** if its average over many samples equals the true value. Dividing the squared gaps by **n - 1** gives an unbiased estimate of the variance. Dividing by **n** gives the maximum-likelihood estimate, which is biased low by the factor (n - 1) / n. Even if S^2 is unbiased, S itself is not.
cards.definition:
For a sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$ from a population with variance $\sigma^2$:

$$S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2,\quad E[S^2]=\sigma^2;\qquad \hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}=\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2,\quad E[\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$$

Bias = E[estimator] minus the true value. E[S] is below σ (Jensen). For a normal mean μ, the sample mean X-bar is unbiased and is also the MLE.
cards.intuition_full: Gaps measured from the sample mean are always a bit smaller than gaps measured from the true mean, because the sample mean is the point that minimises the sum of squared gaps within the sample. In fact, the sum of squared gaps from X-bar equals the sum from μ minus n times (X-bar - μ)^2. Taking expectations, the first part is nσ^2 and the second is σ^2, leaving (n - 1)σ^2. So dividing by n - 1 restores σ^2 exactly. The MLE maximises the likelihood and for a normal sample that gives the divisor n. For the square root: S^2 is unbiased, but the square root is concave, so E[S] is less than the square root of E[S^2] = σ.

example.setup: A sample is 2, 4, 9. Find the sample variance S^2, the MLE of the variance, and explain the bias when the true variance is 12.
steps: Mean = 15 / 3 = 5. Deviations: -3, -1, 4. Squares: 9, 1, 16. Sum of squares = 26.
Unbiased estimate: S^2 = 26 / (n - 1) = 26 / 2 = 13.
If the true variance is 12, the MLE averages (n - 1) / n x 12 = (2 / 3) x 12 = 8, too low, while S^2 averages 12.
S^2 is unbiased, but S = sqrt(13) = 3.61 is not an unbiased estimate of σ: E[S] is below σ.
example.answer: S^2 = 13 and MLE = 8.67. On average the MLE gives 8 when the truth is 12.

cards.title: Reading a confidence level
cards.simple: Suppose a machine makes a measuring tape that traps the true value in 95 out of 100 tries. Each time you use it you get a range. Before you look, there is a 95% chance your range will trap the truth. But once you have a particular range, the truth is either inside it or not. There is no 95% chance left, only the fact that the method works 95% of the time. So '95% confident' is a statement about the method's long-run record, not about this one range. In exam words: the level is the long-run coverage of the method, not the probability that μ lies in one finished interval.
cards.idea: The true mean μ is a fixed number. The interval is what changes from sample to sample. A **95% confidence level** means that if you repeated the experiment many times, about 95% of the intervals you build would contain μ. It is a statement about the **method**, not about one finished interval.
cards.definition:
Let the interval be $(L,U)$ built from the sample. Then

$$P(L<\mu<U)=0.95$$

before the data are seen, where the probability is over the random sample. After the sample is observed, (L, U) is a pair of numbers, and μ is either in it or not.

In n independent repetitions, the number of intervals covering μ is Binomial(n, 0.95).
cards.intuition_full: Think of throwing a ring at a fixed peg. If you throw well enough to ring the peg 95% of the time, then before a throw, there is a 95% chance of success. After the ring has landed, it either surrounds the peg or it does not. The peg does not move and the ring is already on the ground. The confidence interval is the ring and μ is the peg. A higher level, like 99%, is a bigger ring that rings the peg more often. A larger sample is a more skilful thrower whose ring is smaller at the same level. Neither changes the rule that a single finished interval has no probability left.

example.setup: The true mean is fixed at μ = 50. Ten samples each give a 95% interval. Describe what you see and what '95%' means.
steps: The true mean is a fixed line. Each interval is a bar built from a different sample.
Five samples, five bars. Each bar is centred at its own sample mean, so they land in different places. All five cover the line.
Five more samples. One bar misses the line. Nine of the ten intervals caught μ.
If you built 1000 such intervals, you would expect about 950 to cover μ, give or take about 7 (the SD is sqrt(1000 x 0.95 x 0.05) = 6.9).
For one finished interval such as (47.1, 52.9): μ = 50 is either inside or it is not. The 95% describes the method's catch rate.
example.answer: About 95% of intervals cover μ in the long run. A single finished interval has no 95% probability left.

steps: Each day's interval covers μ with probability 0.95, independently.
The number of covering intervals is Binomial(200, 0.95).
Expected number = 200 x 0.95 = 190.
So about 10 of the 200 intervals will miss μ, and that is normal, not a sign of a mistake.

examples.setup: From one sample, the 95% interval for μ is (46.08, 53.92). Is P(46.08 < μ < 53.92) = 0.95? Does the 99% interval from the same data have a higher probability of containing μ?
steps: μ is a fixed number, and the endpoints 46.08 and 53.92 are now fixed numbers too.
So the statement 'P(46.08 < μ < 53.92) = 0.95' has no randomness left. It is either 0 or 1, and we do not know which.
The 99% interval from the same data is wider: 50 plus or minus 2.576 x 2 = (44.85, 55.15).
The 99% method covers μ more often in the long run, 99% versus 95%, but that is also a statement about the method.
More confidence is paid for with width: 10.30 versus 7.84.
examples.answer: No. A finished interval has no probability left. The 99% method has the higher long-run coverage but a wider interval.

cards.why: Misreading the confidence level is the most common conceptual error about intervals. In GATE: pick the correct interpretation of an interval from a list, or count expected coverage over repeated samples.
how: Remember what is random: the sample and so the interval. μ is fixed.
'95%' describes the long-run fraction of intervals that cover μ.
Do not say 'there is a 95% chance μ is in this interval' for numbers already computed.
For repeated intervals use a binomial: n trials, probability equal to the level.
Higher level means wider interval, with n fixed.
cards.mistake: Reading a 95% interval as a 95% chance that μ is in it, once the numbers are computed. Another slip is saying that 95% of the data lie inside the interval: the interval is for the mean, not for individual observations.
edge_cases: 95% of individual observations do not lie in the interval: it is about the mean.
Two independent studies can give different intervals, both valid at 95%.
More confidence means a wider interval, not a more accurate estimate.
About 5% of intervals will miss: seeing a miss does not mean the method is broken.
connections: It is the long-run viewpoint behind p-values and error rates (prob.tests).
The interval formulas are in the z interval and proportion cards.
Counting covering intervals uses the binomial (prob.discrete).

try.label: Which statement about a 95% interval is right

cards.what: The true mean μ is a fixed number. The interval is what changes from sample to sample. A **95% confidence level** means that if you repeated the experiment many times, about 95% of the intervals you build would contain μ. It is a statement about the **method**, not about one finished interval.
cards.what_full:
The true mean μ is a fixed number. The interval is what changes from sample to sample. A **95% confidence level** means that if you repeated the experiment many times, about 95% of the intervals you build would contain μ. It is a statement about the **method**, not about one finished interval.

Let the interval be $(L,U)$ built from the sample. Then

$$P(L<\mu<U)=0.95$$

before the data are seen, where the probability is over the random sample. After the sample is observed, (L, U) is a pair of numbers, and μ is either in it or not.

In n independent repetitions, the number of intervals covering μ is Binomial(n, 0.95).

**Worked example.** The true mean is fixed at μ = 50. Ten samples each give a 95% interval. Describe what you see and what '95%' means.

1. The true mean is a fixed line. Each interval is a bar built from a different sample.
2. Five samples, five bars. Each bar is centred at its own sample mean, so they land in different places. All five cover the line.
3. Five more samples. One bar misses the line. Nine of the ten intervals caught μ.
4. If you built 1000 such intervals, you would expect about 950 to cover μ, give or take about 7 (the SD is sqrt(1000 x 0.95 x 0.05) = 6.9).
5. For one finished interval such as (47.1, 52.9): μ = 50 is either inside or it is not. The 95% describes the method's catch rate.

**Answer:** About 95% of intervals cover μ in the long run. A single finished interval has no 95% probability left.

scenes.title: Sums of dice turn into a bell

steps.caption: One die: all six faces have probability 1/6, a flat shape. Mean 3.5, variance 35/12 = 2.917.
Sum of 2 dice: a triangle from 2 to 12, with 7 the most likely. Mean 7, variance 5.833.
Sum of 3 dice: already a hump from 3 to 18. Mean 10.5, variance 8.75.
Sum of 30 dice: mean 30 x 3.5 = 105, variance 30 x 35/12 = 87.5, SD = 9.354. By the CLT it is close to N(105, 87.5).
'Y <= 20' covers the bars up to 20, whose right edge is 20.5, so use 20.5 as the boundary.
The exact binomial value is 0.9007, so the approximation is within 0.003.

scenes.title: z interval: confidence costs width, data buys narrowness

objects.text: more confidence = wider; more n = narrower

steps.caption: Standard error = σ / sqrt(n) = 12 / 6 = 2.
99%: z = 2.576, half-width = 5.152. Interval = (44.85, 55.15). More confidence, wider interval.
n = 144: SE = 12 / 12 = 1, half-width 1.96. Interval = (48.04, 51.96), half as wide as with n = 36.
Lesson: confidence costs width, and data buys narrowness. Quadrupling n halves the width.

scenes.title: Smallest n for a given margin

objects.text: E = z sigma/sqrt n must be <= 2

steps.caption: Half-width E = z σ / sqrt(n) must be at most 2.
Solve: sqrt(n) >= z σ / E, so n >= (z σ / E)^2.
Round up to the next whole number: n = 107.
Check: n = 106 gives E = 2.576 x 8 / sqrt(106) = 2.0016, just above 2. n = 107 gives E = 1.9923, which is at most 2.
Sample proportion p-hat = 140 / 500 = 0.28.
Interval = 0.28 plus or minus 0.0394 = (0.2406, 0.3194).
Worst case for comparison: with p = 0.5 the SE would be 0.0224 and the margin 0.0438, the largest it can be for n = 500.

scenes.title: Chi-square with 6 degrees of freedom and a sample variance

objects.text: X = Z1^2 + ... + Z6^2, chi-square with 6 df

steps.caption: X is a sum of 6 squared standard normals, so X ~ chi-square with k = 6 degrees of freedom.
Var(X) = 2k = 12, so the SD is 3.46.
For the sample: (n - 1) S^2 / σ^2 = 8 S^2 / 9 ~ chi-square with 8 degrees of freedom. So S^2 = (9 / 8) times a chi-square(8) variable.

scenes.title: t with 8 degrees of freedom against the normal

objects.text: t with 8 df: lower middle, higher tails

steps.caption: The standard normal has a peak 0.399 at 0 and thin tails.
Overlay t with 8 degrees of freedom: it is slightly lower at the middle and higher in the tails.
Beyond +/-2: the normal has 2 x 0.0228 = 0.0455. The t_8 has 0.0805. Heavier tails mean more extreme values.
Variance of t_8 = 8 / (8 - 2) = 1.333, larger than the normal's 1.
For t_30: 30 / 28 = 1.071. With more degrees of freedom it moves close to the normal.

objects.text: S^2 unbiased, but S = 3.61 is biased low

steps.caption: Mean = 15 / 3 = 5. Deviations: -3, -1, 4. Squares: 9, 1, 16. Sum of squares = 26.
Unbiased estimate: S^2 = 26 / (n - 1) = 26 / 2 = 13.
If the true variance is 12, the MLE averages (n - 1) / n x 12 = (2 / 3) x 12 = 8, too low, while S^2 averages 12.
S^2 is unbiased, but S = sqrt(13) = 3.61 is not an unbiased estimate of σ: E[S] is below σ.
